title: Take the Words Out and See What Is Left
scopeNote: This keeps the design decisions, the live recomputation of construct-irrelevant demand and the fictional participants described only by prior exposure to formats. Two of the six decisions, a fourth participant, the explicit construct-relevant share of a score and the closing exercise on comparability evidence stay in the longer version.
summary: Design a reasoning task from four decisions and watch what each one demands beyond reasoning. Taking every word out removes the reading demand and raises two others.
learningObjectives: Explain why removing language does not make a test culture-free.
Recognise that an abstract figure format is itself something a person has met or has not.
Identify the demands that no design decision can remove.
Distinguish reducing an irrelevant demand from establishing that scores are comparable.
Treat unfamiliarity with a format as a fact about exposure rather than about a population.
interactionTypes: a judgement about what removing the words achieves
four design decisions, each moving several demands at once
a live profile of what the design demands beyond reasoning
three fictional people carrying different shares of the same design's demand
a guided move that removes every word and shows what rises
privacy: Nothing is collected, stored or transmitted. No test is administered, no score is produced for anyone, and no difference between any groups is simulated.
accessibilityNotes: Keyboard operable throughout. Design decisions are native radio buttons in labelled fieldsets, and each option's description states in words what it adds to which demands. The demand chart labels a substantial demand in words as well as by colour, and its description lists all six values. The participant table is a real table with row and column headers and names in words where most of each person's demand comes from. Nothing is timed and there is no motion.
dataStatus: Invented demand levels chosen to make the trade-offs legible, not measurements. The three fictional people are described only by prior experience of testing formats, devices and puzzle conventions, and have no nationality, ethnicity, region, language or group membership.
simulationNotes: Six sources of construct-irrelevant demand are tracked on a 0 to 1 scale, and each of the four decisions adds to some of them. Two properties were checked across all eighty-one designs rather than asserted. No design brings every demand below the 0.30 line, and the lowest achievable maximum is exactly 0.30. And exactly two demands have a floor at 0.30 that no decision can go under: knowing how a formal test works, and knowing when to guess and when to move on. Those two were chosen to be the irreducible ones deliberately, because both are things a person learns by having sat tests before, and an earlier version had a third floor that was an artefact of the item options rather than a point about test-taking. The guided move is the demonstration: going from written instructions with verbal items to demonstrated instructions with figure items takes the reading demand from 1.00 to 0.10 and simultaneously takes having-met-abstract-puzzles from 0.40 to 0.85 and knowing-when-to-guess from 0.65 to 0.85. Removing the words does not merely leave the other demands alone; it makes two worse. The three fictional people are described only by prior exposure to formats, and what is reported for each is how much of the design's demand falls on them given what they have had the chance to become familiar with. It is not a score, not a prediction and not an estimate of anybody's reasoning, and the table says so. Simplifications: the numbers are invented, the six demands are not a complete list, and the construct-relevant share of a score that the longer version computes is left out.
readmeTopic: why a test with no words in it still assumes a great deal
